description: The Estée Lauder Companies Inc. manufactures, markets, and sells skin care, makeup, fragrance, and hair care products worldwide. The company provides skin care products, including moisturizers, serums
description_full: The Estée Lauder Companies Inc. manufactures, markets, and sells skin care, makeup, fragrance, and hair care products worldwide. The company provides skin care products, including moisturizers, serums, cleansers, toners, eye care, body care, exfoliators, acne care and oil correctors, facial masks, and sun care products; and makeup products, such as foundations, powders, concealers and setting sprays, lipsticks, lip liners and lip glosses, mascaras, and eyeshadows and eyeliners, as well as compacts, brushes, and other makeup tools. It also offers fragrance products in various forms comprising parfum, eau de parfum, eau de toilette, eau de cologne, and body spray, as well as lotions, creams, powders, candles and soaps; and hair care products, including shampoos, conditioners, styling products, treatment, finishing sprays, and hair color products, as well as sells ancillary products and services. The company provides its products under the La Mer, Jo Malone London, TOM FORD, AERIN Beauty, Le Labo, Editions de Parfums Frédéric Malle, KILIAN PARIS, BALMAIN Beauty, Estée Lauder, Clinique, M·A·C, The Ordinary, Aveda, Bobbi Brown Cosmetics, Too Faced, Dr.Jart+, Bumble and bumble, Smashbox, Darphin Paris, Lab Series, Avestan, Loopha, Origins, NIOD, Aramis, and GLAMGLOW brands. It sells its products through department stores, duty-free retailers, specialty multi retailers, online pure players, upscale perfumeries and pharmacies, and top-tier salons and spas, as well as direct-to-consumer businesses across freestanding stores, and brand websites and third-party online platforms. The Estée Lauder Companies Inc. was founded in 1946 and is based in New York, New York.

financial_summary: Estee Lauder Companies, Inc. (T is a large-cap consumer defensive business with a $39.9B market cap on $15.0B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -2% over the past three years and +3% annually across the full decade — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding.
Returns on capital run at 4% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests. Gross margins of 78% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $1.3B in free cash flow — roughly 9 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 9.74× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -8.1% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 4.6× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 2.3× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Shareholder yield is only 1.4%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 5% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Defensive median (7%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.64x).
It accounts for 0.5% of sector revenue and 0.3% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-23.6% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.07 across 172 companies in the universe; the top four hold 38% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 8% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 10% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 48% and a beta of 1.12, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $297.6M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 34% in the 2020 crash, 49% in the 2022 bear market and 62% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $44.60 (margin of safety -147%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 44%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $31.56 to $62.43 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Defensive peers: P/E 110.1 vs 18.5, EV/EBITDA 17.3 vs 10.3 and P/FCF 30.3 vs 16.0 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 84% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.3% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 1.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 27 covering analysts target $114 on average, 4% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 4% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.1%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.66).
It runs a 78% gross margin and converts 9% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is a concern: high accruals (-8.1% of assets).
ROE of 5% is amplified by 5.2x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 1.4% of revenue on R&D and 2.1% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 4.6x net debt to EBITDA ($3.2B of cash against $7.3B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 2.3x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.3, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at -1.8% over 3 years, -1.5% over 5 years and 2.9% over 10 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -15.2% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a backlog worth 5% of annual revenue and deferred revenue down 10%.
Capex runs only 0.6x depreciation (3.0% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 5, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.3%), and institutions hold 96%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (7 sales, net $11.5M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.4% (0.2% in buybacks and 1.3% in dividends).
It pays out 140% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
people: With about 37,950 employees, each generates about $397K of revenue, 0.8x the Consumer Defensive median, and productivity has risen 3.6% a year.
That works out to $35K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $5.7M (14x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (10/10, lower is better).
